extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof-based calculus and functions
extracted.subtask_short: proofs in calculus: functions and limits
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material giving definitions, theorems, proof techniques, and exercises about functions (composition, inverse, image/preimage) and epsilon–delta limits for real-valued functions. Targets students learning rigorous calculus proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A→B and g:B→C are injective, then g∘f is injective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: g(f(x)) = g(f(y)) implies f(x)=f(y) (since g injective), then x=y (since f injective). This is the direct chain-of-implication proof; include explicit use of each function's injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:A→B and g:B→C are surjective, then g∘f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: For arbitrary c∈C, use surjectivity of g to find b∈B with g(b)=c, then surjectivity of f to find a∈A with f(a)=b; then g(f(a))=c. Shows how existence (rather than uniqueness) is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function
rubrics_metrics.description: For a set A, the identity function i_A:A→A is defined by i_A(x)=x for every x∈A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: i_A is bijective (injective and surjective). It satisfies the equations i_A(x)=x and plays the role of an identity under composition: f∘i_A = f and i_B∘f = f for f:A→B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a relation R from A to B, the inverse relation R^{-1} is {(y,x) : (x,y)∈R}, a relation from B to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: R^{-1} is obtained by swapping coordinates in each ordered pair. Even if R is a function, R^{-1} need not be a function (first-coordinate duplicates may occur). Example illustrations show arrows reversed in diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijectivity ⇔ inverse relation is a function
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f:A→B is bijective if and only if the inverse relation f^{-1} is a function from B to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: If f is bijective then f^{-1} is a function and f^{-1}∘f = i_A and f∘f^{-1} = i_B. Conversely, if f^{-1} (as a relation) is a function, then f must be both injective and surjective. Examples highlight failures when injectivity or surjectivity is missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to compute an inverse function
rubrics_metrics.description: To find f^{-1}, start with y = f(x), interchange variables to get x = f(y), then solve for y to obtain y = f^{-1}(x) when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: solve algebraically (e.g., f(x)=x^3+1 gives f^{-1}(x)=∛(x−1)). Keep careful track of domain/codomain and coordinates for multivariable cases; check by composition f^{-1}(f(x))=x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary properties for inverse relation to be a function
rubrics_metrics.description: For the inverse relation f^{-1} of a function f to be a function, f must be injective and surjective (i.e., bijective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation with counterexample: If f is not injective (two domain elements map to same codomain element), then f^{-1} has duplicate first-coordinates and fails the function property. If f is not surjective, some codomain elements have no preimage, so f^{-1} is not a function from B to A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and preimage (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:A→B, if X⊆A then the image f(X) = { f(x) : x∈X } ⊆ B. If Y⊆B then the preimage f^{-1}(Y) = { x∈A : f(x)∈Y } ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important note: f^{-1}(Y) (the preimage) is defined even when the inverse function does not exist. Distinguish between f^{-1} as preimage operator and f^{-1} as inverse function; the former accepts subsets of B, the latter is a function B→A that exists only when f is bijective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation caution: elements vs subsets in preimage/image
rubrics_metrics.description: The arguments X and Y in f(X) and f^{-1}(Y) must be subsets, not individual elements, when using the set-image/preimage notation; using f^{-1}(4) is ambiguous if the inverse function does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: f^{-1}({4}) as preimage (subset) can be meaningful even if no inverse function exists; but writing f^{-1}(4) to mean the inverse function evaluated at 4 is only valid when f^{-1} (the function) exists. Also note distinction between f({s}) and f(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic image/preimage set identities (Theorem 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Some equalities are one-way inclusions in general (e.g., (1) and (6) need not be equalities unless f is injective/surjective respectively). Exercises ask for proofs and counterexamples; use these to understand when equalities fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: distance between x and y is at most the sum of distances via z. Corollaries used in proofs: |x−y| ≤ |x|+|y|, |x+y| ≤ |x|+|y|, and |x| − |y| ≤ |x+y|. The book uses geometric number-line diagrams and these inequalities frequently in epsilon–delta proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise (ε-δ) definition of limit
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:X→R (X⊆R) and c∈R, lim_{x→c} f(x) = L means: for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that 0<|x−c|<δ implies |f(x)−L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: use 0<|x−c| to exclude x=c in case f(c) undefined. Also require that there exists some δ>0 for which (c−δ,c)∪(c,c+δ) is contained in the domain of f (so f is defined on points arbitrarily close to c). Symbolic form: ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 (0<|x−c|<δ ⇒ |f(x)−L|<ε).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary domain condition for limits to make sense
rubrics_metrics.description: lim_{x→c} f(x) makes sense only if there is some δ>0 such that (c−δ,c)∪(c,c+δ) ⊆ domain(f); i.e., f must be defined on points arbitrarily close to c (excluding possibly c itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the domain has a gap around c, the standard two-sided limit cannot be discussed; right/left limits may be considered separately in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof strategy for limits (finding δ from ε)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lim_{x→c} f(x)=L directly: assume ε>0 and find δ>0 (often by algebraically factoring |x−c| from |f(x)−L|) so that 0<|x−c|<δ ⇒ |f(x)−L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: manipulate |f(x)−L| to isolate a factor of |x−c|; if extra factors remain, bound them by restricting δ (e.g., ensure |x−c|≤1 so x near c gives bounds on other terms). Examples given for linear and quadratic polynomials illustrate this pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways a limit can fail to exist and proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A limit may fail because: (i) left/right behavior approaches different numbers, or (ii) function oscillates and approaches no number (e.g., sin(1/x) near 0). To prove nonexistence, assume lim_{x→c} f(x)=L and derive a contradiction (often by choosing ε and showing no δ can satisfy the definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: piecewise functions with different one-sided affine formulas; oscillatory example sin(1/x) uses sequences x_k giving distinct cluster behaviors and yields contradiction by choosing ε suitably (e.g., 1/2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard limit laws (constant, identity, scalar multiple, sum, difference, product)
rubrics_metrics.description: If relevant limits exist, the following hold: constant function lim_{x→c} a = a; identity lim_{x→c} x = c; scalar multiple lim_{x→c} a f(x) = a lim_{x→c} f(x); sum lim_{x→c} (f+g) = lim f + lim g; difference analogous; product lim (f g) = (lim f)(lim g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof techniques: use triangle inequality variants and previous laws; for sum use splitting |f+g−(L+M)| ≤ |f−L|+|g−M| and choose δ as min of δ's for f and g. For product handle terms by adding/subtracting L g(x) and using bounds on g(x) near c; often require bounding g(x) within some range by restricting δ.
